key_insight: Modeling futures as sparse interacting point trajectories (instead of dense pixels or latent frames) lets you cheaply sample many plausible long-horizon scenarios and represent uncertainty more effectively.
problem_solved: Reduces computational cost and improves long-horizon multi-hypothesis prediction by shifting capacity from dense appearance prediction to sparse, trajectory-centric simulation of scene dynamics.
method: Represent scene dynamics as sparse sets of points (trajectories) that capture object and interaction structure rather than dense video frames.
Learn stochastic transition models that roll out long interaction chains and efficiently sample many plausible futures to capture uncertainty and multimodality.
Prioritize capacity for trajectory exploration and interaction modeling so large-scale hypothesis generation is tractable for downstream planning/evaluation.
impact: Enables scalable, uncertainty-aware long-horizon forecasting useful for planning and decision-making in robotics, autonomous driving, and simulation—reducing compute and improving actionable predictions.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram: dense video prediction vs. sparse trajectory prediction highlighting reduced complexity and focus on motion.
Pipeline flowchart: input scene → sparse point extraction → stochastic transition model → multi-hypothesis rollouts.
Fan/riverplot of multiple sampled futures (trajectories) illustrating multimodality and uncertainty over time.
Bar or scatter chart comparing computation cost (e.g., FLOPs or memory) and long-horizon accuracy/consistency for dense vs. sparse approaches.
paper_title: Envisioning the Future, One Step at a Time
paper_authors: Stefan Andreas Baumann, Jannik Wiese, Tommaso Martorella, Mahdi M. Kalayeh, Björn Ommer
